reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: A non-hereditary disorder of multiple enchondromas caused by post-zygotic somatic mosaic variants in IDH1 or IDH2, so it is sporadic rather than inherited
Enchondromas are intramedullary cartilaginous lesions that characteristically show an asymmetric, often unilateral distribution across the body
Predominantly affects the metaphyses and diaphyses of the hands, feet and long bones, causing swelling, deformity and limb-length discrepancy
Radiographs show radiolucent intramedullary lesions with characteristic linear or stippled calcification and cortical expansion
Pathological fracture through a lesion is a common presentation
Malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is a recognised long-term risk, higher than in solitary enchondroma and increasing with lesion number
Distinguish from multiple hereditary exostoses, where the lesions are surface osteochondromas rather than intramedullary enchondromas
reference.pathophysiology: Ollier disease arises from somatic mosaic gain-of-function variants in the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes IDH1 or IDH2, occurring in a subset of cells during development. Mutant IDH enzymes produce the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which disturbs DNA and histone methylation and blocks normal chondrocyte differentiation. Islands of residual growth-plate cartilage persist and continue to proliferate within the medullary cavity as enchondromas rather than being resorbed and replaced by bone. The mosaic origin explains the asymmetric distribution and the absence of vertical transmission.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey to map the distribution and burden of enchondromas
MRI of symptomatic or enlarging lesions to assess cartilage and aggressive features
Consideration of somatic IDH1/IDH2 testing on lesional tissue where diagnosis is uncertain
Imaging surveillance for change in size, cortical breach or soft-tissue mass
Biopsy of any lesion with features suspicious for malignant transformation
redFlags: New pain or growth of a previously stable lesion suggesting malignant transformation
Cortical destruction or an associated soft-tissue mass on imaging
Rapidly progressive deformity or functional impairment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on lesion number, size and site; morbidity comes from deformity, limb-length discrepancy and fracture, while the principal serious concern is malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma, warranting lifelong surveillance.
pitfalls: Assuming an inherited disorder and giving incorrect recurrence-risk counselling, when the condition is sporadic and mosaic
Failing to arrange surveillance for malignant transformation
Confusing intramedullary enchondromas with the surface osteochondromas of hereditary exostoses
Missing an associated haemangioma that would reclassify the disorder as Maffucci syndrome
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Orphanet / WHO Classification of Tumours: Enchondromatosis (Ollier disease)
management: No medical therapy exists for the enchondromas themselves; management combines surveillance with orthopaedic treatment of complications
Orthopaedic surgery for deformity, pathological fracture and limb-length discrepancy, including curettage and grafting, corrective osteotomy and limb equalisation or lengthening
Lifelong clinical and imaging surveillance for malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma, prompted by new pain, growth, cortical breach or a soft-tissue mass
Prompt MRI and biopsy of any lesion with aggressive features, proceeding to wide excision if chondrosarcoma is confirmed
Baseline skeletal survey to map lesion burden and distribution
Multidisciplinary care across orthopaedics, radiology and a specialist bone-tumour or sarcoma service
Reassurance that the disorder is a sporadic somatic-mosaic IDH1/IDH2 condition and not inherited, so routine familial genetic screening is unnecessary
